blocks.en: "And if Christ is not risen, then our preaching is empty and your faith is also empty." — 1 Corinthians 15:14
blocks.es_reference: "Y si Cristo no resucitó, vana es entonces nuestra predicación, vana es también vuestra fe." — 1 Corintios 15:14 (RVG)

blocks.en: The Hinge of Everything
blocks.es_reference: El Eje de Todo

blocks.en: Of all the religions on earth, Christianity is the only one that hands its critics a sword and says, here, this is where you may strike me dead. Paul put it without a hedge: if Christ is not risen, then our preaching is empty and your faith is empty too. He did not say the faith would limp along as a lovely philosophy if the tomb were full; he said it would be finished, and that we who preach it would be exposed as liars. The teachings of the Buddha do not stand or fall on whether his bones lie in a grave, and Islam does not rest its case on an empty tomb. But the whole weight of Christianity hangs on a single event in history: that a dead man walked out of a sealed grave on the third day. This makes ours the most testable faith in the world, the one most open to disproof. Produce the body and you have won the argument forever. So we need not be afraid of this question. Let us walk straight up to the grave and look inside.
blocks.es_reference: De todas las religiones de la tierra, el cristianismo es la única que entrega una espada a sus críticos y dice, aquí, este es el lugar donde puedes darme muerte. Pablo lo dijo sin rodeos: si Cristo no resucitó, vana es entonces nuestra predicación, y vana también vuestra fe. No dijo que la fe seguiría cojeando como una bella filosofía si la tumba estuviera llena; dijo que estaría acabada, y que los que la predicamos quedaríamos expuestos como mentirosos. Las enseñanzas de Buda no se sostienen ni caen según yazgan sus huesos en una tumba, y el islam no apoya su caso en un sepulcro vacío. Pero todo el peso del cristianismo pende de un solo evento en la historia: que un hombre muerto salió de una tumba sellada al tercer día. Esto hace que la nuestra sea la fe más comprobable del mundo, la más abierta a ser refutada. Presente el cuerpo y habrá ganado el argumento para siempre. Así que no necesitamos temer esta pregunta. Vayamos derecho hasta la tumba y miremos adentro.

blocks.en: What Must Be Explained
blocks.es_reference: Lo que Debe Explicarse

blocks.en: An honest investigator does not begin with a verdict; he begins with the facts that any theory must explain. Here are facts that even most skeptical historians grant. Jesus of Nazareth was executed by Roman crucifixion and was certainly dead. His tomb was found empty on the third day. His followers were suddenly and unshakably convinced that they had seen Him alive, touched Him, and eaten with Him. And within a few weeks the church exploded into life in Jerusalem — the one city on earth where the whole thing could have been crushed in an afternoon simply by walking to the tomb and producing a body. No body was ever produced. Stranger still is the sociological shift that followed. Jews who had kept the seventh-day Sabbath for fifteen centuries began, within the lifetime of the earliest church, to give special significance to the first day of the week, the day He rose — a change that took hold within a generation or two, even as many Jewish believers continued for years to participate in synagogue and temple life alongside it. Men raised to recoil at the thought of a crucified Messiah, a contradiction in their own terms, began proclaiming a crucified Messiah as Lord and God. Something happened that bent the course of history, and every theory must account for all of it at once.
blocks.es_reference: Un investigador honesto no comienza con un veredicto; comienza con los hechos que toda teoría debe explicar. He aquí hechos que aun la mayoría de los historiadores escépticos conceden. Jesús de Nazaret fue ejecutado por crucifixión romana y estaba ciertamente muerto. Su tumba fue hallada vacía al tercer día. Sus seguidores quedaron de repente e inquebrantablemente convencidos de que lo habían visto vivo, lo habían tocado y habían comido con Él. Y en pocas semanas la iglesia estalló a la vida en Jerusalén — la única ciudad de la tierra donde todo el asunto pudo haberse aplastado en una tarde con solo caminar hasta la tumba y presentar un cuerpo. Jamás se presentó ningún cuerpo. Más extraño todavía es el cambio sociológico que siguió. Judíos que habían guardado el sábado del séptimo día por quince siglos comenzaron, dentro de la vida de la iglesia primitiva, a dar un significado especial al primer día de la semana, el día en que Él resucitó — un cambio que se afianzó en una generación o dos, aun cuando muchos creyentes judíos siguieron participando por años en la vida de la sinagoga y del templo junto con esa nueva práctica. Hombres criados para estremecerse ante la idea de un Mesías crucificado, una contradicción en sus propios términos, comenzaron a proclamar a un Mesías crucificado como Señor y Dios. Algo sucedió que dobló el curso de la historia, y toda teoría debe dar cuenta de todo ello a la vez.

blocks.en: The Reluctant Witnesses
blocks.es_reference: Los Testigos Renuentes

blocks.en: The heart of the case is not the believers who wanted it to be true, but the witnesses who did not. The law has always known that the testimony worth most is the hostile witness, the one with every reason to say no. The resurrection produced three of them. First, the Skeptic. Thomas had walked with Jesus for years, yet when the others said the Lord was risen, he flatly refused to believe on their word: unless I touch the wounds, he said, I will not believe. Then he met the risen Christ, and the doubter who demanded proof fell down and said, "My Lord and my God." Second, the Enemy. Saul of Tarsus was no seeker; he was the church's chief persecutor, breathing threats, dragging believers to prison, holding the coats of those who stoned Stephen. He had everything to gain by destroying the movement and everything to lose by joining it. Yet on the Damascus road the risen Christ stopped him in his tracks, and the enemy became the apostle who would suffer and die for the name he had tried to erase. Third, the Family. James was the brother of Jesus, raised in the same house, and the Gospels admit with embarrassing honesty that during Jesus' life His own brothers did not believe in Him. But after the resurrection this same James stands as the leader of the Jerusalem church, and later dies a martyr for Him — a death reported not only by Christian sources but by the Jewish historian Josephus, giving it unusually strong outside corroboration for a first-century martyrdom. Ask yourself what it would take to convince you that your own brother was the Lord of glory. James was convinced — by seeing Him raised.
blocks.es_reference: El corazón del caso no son los creyentes que querían que fuera verdad, sino los testigos que no lo querían. La ley siempre ha sabido que el testimonio que más vale es el del testigo hostil, el que tiene toda razón para decir que no. La resurrección produjo tres de ellos. Primero, el Escéptico. Tomás había caminado con Jesús por años, y sin embargo cuando los otros dijeron que el Señor había resucitado, rehusó rotundamente creer por la palabra de ellos: a menos que toque las heridas, dijo, no creeré. Entonces se encontró con el Cristo resucitado, y el que dudaba y exigía pruebas cayó y dijo: "Señor mío, y Dios mío." Segundo, el Enemigo. Saulo de Tarso no era un buscador; era el principal perseguidor de la iglesia, respirando amenazas, arrastrando creyentes a la cárcel, guardando los mantos de los que apedrearon a Esteban. Tenía todo que ganar destruyendo el movimiento y todo que perder uniéndose a él. Sin embargo, en el camino de Damasco el Cristo resucitado lo detuvo en seco, y el enemigo se volvió el apóstol que sufriría y moriría por el nombre que había tratado de borrar. Tercero, la Familia. Jacobo era el hermano de Jesús, criado en la misma casa, y los Evangelios admiten con vergonzosa honestidad que durante la vida de Jesús sus propios hermanos no creían en Él. Pero después de la resurrección este mismo Jacobo está como líder de la iglesia de Jerusalén, y más tarde muere mártir por Él — una muerte reportada no solo por fuentes cristianas sino por el historiador judío Josefo, lo cual le da una corroboración externa inusualmente fuerte para un martirio del siglo primero. Pregúntese qué se necesitaría para convencerlo de que su propio hermano era el Señor de gloria. Jacobo fue convencido — por verlo resucitado.

blocks.en: They Will Not Die for What They Know Is a Lie
blocks.es_reference: No Morirán por lo que Saben Que Es Mentira

blocks.en: Now press on the obvious objection: people will die for all sorts of beliefs, so what does the death of the apostles prove? Here we must be careful and exact. It is true that men in every age have died for things that were false; a man will lay down his life for a lie if he sincerely believes it to be true. But that is not the situation of the apostles. They were not deceived followers a thousand miles from the event; they were the very men who would have known, beyond any possibility of mistake, whether they had seen the risen Lord or had stolen His body and invented the tale. You might die for a lie you believe is true. You will not die for a lie you know is a lie. And these men, given every chance to save their lives by recanting, went to prison, to the whip, and to the executioner still insisting on what they had seen with their eyes and touched with their hands. Liars make poor martyrs once the dying starts.
blocks.es_reference: Ahora presione la objeción obvia: la gente muere por toda clase de creencias, así que ¿qué prueba la muerte de los apóstoles? Aquí debemos ser cuidadosos y exactos. Es verdad que hombres de toda época han muerto por cosas que eran falsas; un hombre dará su vida por una mentira si sinceramente cree que es verdad. Pero esa no es la situación de los apóstoles. No eran seguidores engañados a mil millas del evento; eran los hombres mismos que habrían sabido, más allá de toda posibilidad de error, si habían visto al Señor resucitado o habían robado su cuerpo e inventado el cuento. Usted puede morir por una mentira que cree verdad. No morirá por una mentira que sabe que es mentira. Y estos hombres, teniendo toda oportunidad de salvar la vida retractándose, fueron a la cárcel, al azote y al verdugo todavía insistiendo en lo que habían visto con sus ojos y tocado con sus manos. Los mentirosos hacen pobres mártires una vez que empieza el morir.

blocks.en: The Collapse of Conspiracies
blocks.es_reference: El Derrumbe de las Conspiraciones

blocks.en: Charles Colson, who stood near the top of American power in the Nixon White House, offered a helpful analogy from bitter experience — not proof of the resurrection, but a way of testing our intuitions about conspiracies. A dozen of the most powerful men in the world, he said, could not hold a simple lie together for even a few weeks once their own skins were on the line; under the pressure of investigation the conspiracy of Watergate fell apart almost at once, each man scrambling to save himself. Colson then asked how twelve frightened fishermen and tax collectors could have held a far greater lie together for decades, across years of beatings and prisons and executions, with not one of them ever breaking to buy his freedom with a confession. The analogy is not evidence that the resurrection happened; it is a way of testing whether "the disciples made it up and then died for the lie" is psychologically plausible, given what we know about how ordinary conspiracies tend to unravel under pressure. Judged that way, the theft-and-cover-up explanation looks considerably less likely than the alternative: that the apostles were telling the truth about what they had seen.
blocks.es_reference: Charles Colson, que estuvo cerca de la cima del poder estadounidense en la Casa Blanca de Nixon, ofreció una analogía útil desde la amarga experiencia — no una prueba de la resurrección, sino una manera de poner a prueba nuestras intuiciones sobre las conspiraciones. Una docena de los hombres más poderosos del mundo, dijo, no pudieron mantener juntos una simple mentira ni por unas pocas semanas una vez que su propio pellejo estuvo en juego; bajo la presión de la investigación la conspiración de Watergate se vino abajo casi de inmediato, cada hombre apurándose a salvarse a sí mismo. Entonces Colson preguntó cómo pudieron doce pescadores y cobradores de impuestos asustados mantener juntos una mentira mucho mayor por décadas, a través de años de golpes y prisiones y ejecuciones, sin que ni uno de ellos jamás se quebrara para comprar su libertad con una confesión. La analogía no es evidencia de que la resurrección sucedió; es una manera de poner a prueba si "los discípulos lo inventaron y luego murieron por la mentira" es psicológicamente creíble, dado lo que sabemos sobre cómo suelen desmoronarse las conspiraciones ordinarias bajo presión. Juzgada así, la explicación del robo y el encubrimiento parece considerablemente menos probable que la alternativa: que los apóstoles decían la verdad sobre lo que habían visto.

blocks.en: The Skeptics Who Set Out to Disprove It
blocks.es_reference: Los Escépticos que Se Propusieron Refutarlo

blocks.en: There is a pattern in the history of this question that ought to give a thoughtful doubter pause: those who have examined the evidence most closely, intending to bury it, have an unsettling habit of changing sides. In the eighteenth century two learned Englishmen, Gilbert West and Lord Lyttelton, agreed to examine what they considered the two weakest-looking pillars of Christianity, the resurrection and the conversion of Paul, each expecting his own study to expose the claim as false. They worked separately and compared results. Each had instead been driven by the evidence to conclude that the event he examined was genuine — West concerning the resurrection, Lyttelton concerning Paul's conversion — and each published a book defending the very claim he had set out to dispute. A century and more later, a writer using the pen name Frank Morison sat down to write a book disproving the resurrection once and for all; the book he actually wrote, after following the facts, argued that it had happened, and he called its opening chapter "the book that refused to be written." In our own day skeptical investigators have repeated the experiment, sitting down to refute and rising up persuaded. It is the modern echo of Thomas: when an honest mind looks long and hard at the testimony, the heart at last bows down.
blocks.es_reference: Hay un patrón en la historia de esta cuestión que debería dar que pensar a un dudoso reflexivo: quienes han examinado la evidencia más de cerca, con la intención de enterrarla, tienen la inquietante costumbre de cambiar de bando. En el siglo dieciocho dos ingleses instruidos, Gilbert West y Lord Lyttelton, acordaron examinar lo que consideraban los dos pilares de apariencia más débil del cristianismo, la resurrección y la conversión de Pablo, cada uno esperando que su propio estudio expusiera la afirmación como falsa. Trabajaron por separado y compararon resultados. Cada uno, en cambio, había sido llevado por la evidencia a concluir que el suceso que examinaba era genuino — West en cuanto a la resurrección, Lyttelton en cuanto a la conversión de Pablo — y cada uno publicó un libro defendiendo la misma afirmación que se había propuesto refutar. Un siglo y más después, un escritor que usaba el seudónimo Frank Morison se sentó a escribir un libro que refutara la resurrección de una vez por todas; el libro que en realidad escribió, tras seguir los hechos, sostenía que había sucedido, y llamó a su capítulo inicial "el libro que rehusó ser escrito." En nuestros propios días, investigadores escépticos han repetido el experimento, sentándose a refutar y levantándose persuadidos. Es el eco moderno de Tomás: cuando una mente honesta mira larga y duramente el testimonio, el corazón al fin se inclina.

blocks.en: The Witnesses Who Would Not Recant
blocks.es_reference: Los Testigos que No Se Retractaron

blocks.en: From that first generation the line of witnesses has never broken. Peter, who once denied his Lord by a fire, was, by the early accounts, crucified at last in Rome, asking to be hung head downward because he counted himself unworthy to die as his Master had. And the centuries since have only added names. Richard Wurmbrand, a Jewish atheist who came to Christ in 1938, spent fourteen years in communist prisons, much of it in torture and solitary confinement, and came out not bitter but praying for his torturers, founding a work for the persecuted church. Here, though, we must keep an honest distinction, for it matters. The apostles are evidence in a way that no later martyr can be, because the apostles were in a position to know firsthand whether the event was real, and the later martyrs were not. Wurmbrand did not see the empty tomb. What the long parade of martyrs proves is not the event itself but its living power: that nineteen centuries after the stone was rolled away, the risen Christ is still so real to men and women that they will suffer anything rather than deny Him. The apostles testify that it happened; the martyrs testify that He is still alive to make such people.
blocks.es_reference: Desde aquella primera generación la línea de testigos nunca se ha roto. Pedro, que una vez negó a su Señor junto a un fuego, fue, según los relatos antiguos, crucificado al fin en Roma, pidiendo ser colgado cabeza abajo porque se contaba indigno de morir como su Maestro. Y los siglos transcurridos solo han añadido nombres. Richard Wurmbrand, un ateo judío que vino a Cristo en 1938, pasó catorce años en prisiones comunistas, mucho de ello en tortura y aislamiento, y salió no amargado sino orando por sus torturadores, fundando una obra para la iglesia perseguida. Aquí, sin embargo, debemos guardar una distinción honesta, porque importa. Los apóstoles son evidencia de un modo que ningún mártir posterior puede serlo, porque los apóstoles estaban en posición de saber de primera mano si el evento era real, y los mártires posteriores no lo estaban. Wurmbrand no vio la tumba vacía. Lo que la larga procesión de mártires prueba no es el evento mismo sino su poder vivo: que diecinueve siglos después de que la piedra fue removida, el Cristo resucitado es todavía tan real para hombres y mujeres que sufrirán cualquier cosa antes que negarlo. Los apóstoles testifican que sucedió; los mártires testifican que Él sigue vivo para hacer tales personas.

blocks.en: The Best Explanation
blocks.es_reference: La Mejor Explicación

blocks.en: Lay all the facts on the table and weigh the explanations honestly. Did the disciples steal the body and then die for what they knew was a fraud? We have seen that liars do not die that way. Did Jesus merely swoon and revive in the cool of the tomb? A man flogged to ribbons and pierced through the heart does not roll back a stone and overpower guards and convince hardened skeptics that He is the conqueror of death. Were the appearances mere hallucinations? Hallucinations are typically private and idiosyncratic to the person having them; the hallucination hypothesis struggles to explain, all at once, appearances reported to individuals and to groups together, the empty-tomb tradition alongside the appearances, and the conversions of hostile figures like Saul and skeptical family members like James. Was it all a legend that grew with the years? Legends need generations to grow, but this proclamation was preached in Jerusalem within weeks, while hostile witnesses who could have refuted it were still alive. Every natural explanation struggles somewhere, and especially on the changed skeptics. The simplest explanation that accounts for the empty tomb, the appearances, the converted enemies, the explosive church, and the unbreakable witness is the one the witnesses themselves gave: He is risen.
blocks.es_reference: Ponga todos los hechos sobre la mesa y sopese las explicaciones con honestidad. ¿Robaron los discípulos el cuerpo y luego murieron por lo que sabían que era un fraude? Hemos visto que los mentirosos no mueren así. ¿Acaso Jesús solo se desmayó y revivió en el frescor de la tumba? Un hombre azotado a jirones y atravesado por el corazón no rueda una piedra ni vence a los guardias ni convence a escépticos endurecidos de que es el vencedor de la muerte. ¿Fueron las apariciones meras alucinaciones? Las alucinaciones suelen ser privadas e idiosincráticas de la persona que las tiene; la hipótesis de la alucinación tiene dificultad para explicar, todo a la vez, las apariciones reportadas a individuos y a grupos juntos, la tradición de la tumba vacía junto con las apariciones, y las conversiones de figuras hostiles como Saulo y de familiares escépticos como Jacobo. ¿Fue todo una leyenda que creció con los años? Las leyendas necesitan generaciones para crecer, pero esta proclamación se predicó en Jerusalén en pocas semanas, mientras testigos hostiles que pudieron haberla refutado seguían vivos. Toda explicación natural tiene dificultades en algún punto, y especialmente ante los escépticos cambiados. La explicación más sencilla que da cuenta de la tumba vacía, las apariciones, los enemigos convertidos, la iglesia explosiva y el testimonio inquebrantable es la que los testigos mismos dieron: Él ha resucitado.

blocks.en: How Early Is the Resurrection Message?
blocks.es_reference: ¿Qué Tan Temprano Es el Mensaje de la Resurrección?

blocks.en: One of the strongest answers to the claim that the resurrection was a late legend is found in 1 Corinthians 15:3–7. Paul wrote 1 Corinthians within the lifetime of many people who had known the earliest Christian movement, but he says the resurrection message was something he had already “received” and then “delivered.” He names Peter, the Twelve, James, the apostles, and more than five hundred witnesses. Scholars differ over exactly how early the wording took shape, but there is broad agreement that the tradition itself is earlier than the letter. The important point is simple: Christians did not wait for generations to begin proclaiming that Jesus died, was buried, rose, and appeared to witnesses. The resurrection was at the center of the message from the beginning. That does not by itself prove that the resurrection happened, but it removes the easy explanation that the story first developed centuries later.
blocks.es_reference: Una de las respuestas más fuertes a la afirmación de que la resurrección fue una leyenda tardía se encuentra en 1 Corintios 15:3–7. Pablo escribió 1 Corintios cuando todavía vivían muchas personas que habían conocido el movimiento cristiano primitivo, pero dice que el mensaje de la resurrección era algo que él ya había “recibido” y luego “entregado”. Nombra a Pedro, a los Doce, a Jacobo, a los apóstoles y a más de quinientos testigos. Los estudiosos difieren sobre la fecha exacta en que tomó forma la redacción, pero existe amplio acuerdo en que la tradición misma es anterior a la carta. El punto importante es sencillo: los cristianos no esperaron generaciones para comenzar a proclamar que Jesús murió, fue sepultado, resucitó y apareció a testigos. La resurrección estuvo en el centro del mensaje desde el principio. Esto por sí solo no demuestra que la resurrección ocurrió, pero elimina la explicación fácil de que la historia surgió por primera vez siglos después.

blocks.en: The Father's Amen
blocks.es_reference: El Amén del Padre

blocks.en: The resurrection is the Father's great Amen spoken over the claims of His Son. Every "I AM" Jesus uttered, every sin He forgave, every promise He made hung unproven until the third day; the empty tomb is heaven's receipt, God's own signature certifying that the bill was paid and the claims were true. And yet, as with every clue in this course, the evidence carries us only to the door. Thomas was given his proof and believed, but the Lord turned from him to us across the centuries and said, "Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed." The empty tomb does not force a man to his knees; it invites him. It clears away every honest excuse and leaves the seeker standing where Thomas once stood, the wounds within reach, the question waiting. Who do you say that He is?
blocks.es_reference: La resurrección es el gran Amén del Padre pronunciado sobre las afirmaciones de su Hijo. Cada "YO SOY" que Jesús pronunció, cada pecado que perdonó, cada promesa que hizo quedó sin probar hasta el tercer día; la tumba vacía es el recibo del cielo, la firma misma de Dios que certifica que la cuenta fue pagada y las afirmaciones eran verdad. Y sin embargo, como con cada pista de este curso, la evidencia nos lleva solo hasta la puerta. A Tomás se le dio su prueba y creyó, pero el Señor se volvió de él hacia nosotros a través de los siglos y dijo: "Bienaventurados los que no vieron, y creyeron." La tumba vacía no obliga a un hombre a arrodillarse; lo invita. Despeja toda excusa honesta y deja al que busca parado donde Tomás una vez estuvo, las heridas al alcance, la pregunta esperando. ¿Quién dice usted que es Él?

blocks.en: "Because you have seen Me, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed." — John 20:29
blocks.es_reference: "Porque me has visto, Tomás, creíste; bienaventurados los que no vieron, y creyeron." — Juan 20:29 (RVG)

sa.prompt: Why does Paul stake everything on the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:14), and what makes Christianity uniquely testable?
sa.model: Paul stakes everything on the resurrection because in 1 Corinthians 15:14 he says that if Christ is not risen, then our preaching is empty and our faith is empty too. He does not treat the faith as a beautiful philosophy that survives an empty claim; he says it is finished if the tomb is full, and that those who preach it are liars. This is what makes Christianity uniquely testable, for it is staked entirely on a single event in history, that a dead man walked out of a sealed tomb on the third day. Other religions do not rise or fall on a grave, but ours does, which means anyone could end the argument forever simply by producing the body. Because no body was ever produced, the unit invites us to walk up to the grave and look honestly inside.

sa.prompt: What facts must any honest explanation of the first Easter account for?
sa.model: The unit lists facts that even most skeptical historians grant and that any theory must explain together. Jesus was executed by Roman crucifixion and was certainly dead. His tomb was found empty on the third day. His followers were suddenly convinced they had seen Him alive, touched Him, and eaten with Him, the appearances. Within weeks the church exploded in Jerusalem, the one city where producing a body would have crushed it at once. And a sociological earthquake followed: Jews who had kept the Sabbath for fifteen centuries began worshiping on Sunday, the day He rose, and men who recoiled at a crucified Messiah began proclaiming one as Lord. An honest investigator must account for all of these at once, not pick and choose.

sa.prompt: Explain the three reluctant witnesses — Thomas, Paul, and James — and why hostile witnesses matter.
sa.model: The heart of the case is the witnesses who did not want it to be true, since the law has always known the hostile witness counts most. The first is Thomas the Skeptic, who refused to believe the others and demanded to touch the wounds, then met the risen Christ and cried, my Lord and my God. The second is Paul the Enemy, Saul of Tarsus, the church's chief persecutor who had everything to lose by joining; the risen Christ stopped him on the Damascus road and turned the enemy into an apostle who suffered and died for the name. The third is James, the brother of Jesus, who did not believe during Jesus' life yet after the resurrection led the Jerusalem church and died for Him. These reluctant and hostile witnesses are powerful precisely because they had every reason to say no, and were convinced only by seeing Him raised.

sa.prompt: Explain 'you will not die for a lie you know is a lie,' and why the apostles' deaths carry evidential weight.
sa.model: The unit answers carefully that people do die for false beliefs, but only when they sincerely believe them to be true; you may die for a lie you believe is true, but you will not die for a lie you know is a lie. The apostles were not deceived followers far from the events; they were the very men who would have known beyond any mistake whether they had seen the risen Lord or had stolen the body and invented the story. Given every chance to save their lives by recanting, they went to prison, the whip, and the executioner still insisting on what they had seen and touched. This is why their deaths carry evidential weight that ordinary martyrdom does not: liars make poor martyrs once the dying starts, so their refusal to recant is strong evidence they were telling the truth.

sa.prompt: Explain Charles Colson's conspiracy point drawn from Watergate.
sa.model: Charles Colson, who stood near the top of power in the Nixon White House, offered this as an analogy from bitter firsthand experience, not as proof of the resurrection but as a way to test our intuitions about conspiracies. A dozen of the most powerful men in the world, he said, could not hold a simple lie together for even a few weeks once their own skins were at risk; under the pressure of investigation the Watergate conspiracy shattered almost at once, each man scrambling to save himself. Colson then asked how twelve frightened fishermen and tax collectors could have kept a far greater secret for decades, through beatings, prisons, and executions, without one of them breaking to buy his freedom with a confession. The analogy does not prove the resurrection; it tests whether the theft-and-cover-up theory is psychologically believable given how ordinary conspiracies actually behave under pressure, and by that test the theory looks weak while the apostles' own explanation looks strong.

sa.prompt: Tell the story of West and Lyttelton and explain what it shows.
sa.model: In the eighteenth century two learned Englishmen, Gilbert West and Lord Lyttelton, agreed to examine what they considered the two weakest-looking pillars of Christianity, the resurrection and the conversion of Paul, each expecting his own study to expose the claim as false. They worked separately and compared their results. Each had instead been driven by the evidence to conclude that the event he examined was genuine — West concerning the resurrection, Lyttelton concerning Paul's conversion — and each published a book defending the very claim he had set out to dispute. The story shows that when a mind that expects to disprove a claim examines the evidence closely, the facts can carry it to the opposite conclusion. It is a modern echo of Thomas: those who look hardest at the testimony often end up persuaded by it, which is why the unit holds it up as encouragement to investigate rather than fear the question.

sa.prompt: Explain the pattern of skeptics who investigated to disprove the resurrection (such as Frank Morison).
sa.model: The unit points to a recurring pattern among those who studied the resurrection meaning to disprove it. Frank Morison, the pen name of an English writer, sat down to write a book that would refute the resurrection once and for all, but after following the evidence the book he actually wrote argued that it had happened, and he titled its opening chapter the book that refused to be written. Other skeptical investigators in our own day have repeated the same experiment, sitting down to refute the claim and rising up persuaded by what they found. The pattern is the modern echo of Thomas: an honest mind that looks long and hard at the testimony is often moved against its first intentions until the heart bows. So the unit treats serious investigation not as a threat to faith but as a path many have walked straight into it.

sa.prompt: Explain the honest distinction between the apostolic witnesses and later martyrs like Wurmbrand.
sa.model: The unit keeps a careful distinction that matters. The apostles are evidence in a way no later martyr can be, because the apostles were in a position to know firsthand whether the resurrection was real, while later martyrs were not. Richard Wurmbrand, a Jewish atheist who came to Christ and endured fourteen years of communist prison and torture, did not see the empty tomb. So the long parade of martyrs through the centuries does not prove the event itself; what it proves is its living power, that nineteen centuries after the stone was rolled away the risen Christ is still so real that people will suffer anything rather than deny Him. The apostles testify that it happened; the later martyrs testify that He is still alive to make such people. Confusing the two would weaken the argument, so the unit holds them apart.

sa.prompt: Why does the unit conclude 'He rose' is the best explanation compared to the alternatives?
sa.model: The unit weighs the natural alternatives and shows each one has serious difficulties. If the disciples stole the body, they would not have died for what they knew was a fraud. If Jesus merely swooned and revived, a man flogged and pierced through the heart could not roll back the stone, overpower guards, and convince hardened skeptics He had conquered death. If the appearances were hallucinations, the hallucination hypothesis struggles to explain, all at once, appearances reported to individuals and to groups, the empty-tomb tradition alongside the appearances, and the conversion of enemies like Saul and skeptical brothers like James. If it was a slow legend, legends need generations, yet this was preached in Jerusalem within weeks while hostile witnesses still lived. Every natural explanation struggles somewhere, especially on the changed skeptics, so the simplest explanation that accounts for the empty tomb, the appearances, the converted enemies, and the unbreakable witness is the one the witnesses gave: He rose.

sa.prompt: What does the resurrection prove about Jesus' claims, and where does it leave the seeker?
sa.model: The unit calls the resurrection the Father's great Amen spoken over the claims of His Son. Every I AM Jesus uttered, every sin He forgave, and every promise He made hung unproven until the third day, and the empty tomb is heaven's receipt, God's own signature certifying that the claims were true. Yet, as with every clue in the course, the evidence carries us only to the door. Thomas was given his proof and believed, but the Lord turned to us across the centuries and said, blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed. The empty tomb does not force a person to his knees; it invites him. It clears away every honest excuse and leaves the seeker standing where Thomas stood, the wounds within reach and the question waiting, who do you say that He is.
